audioscript.text: So, is there anything else to do over on that side of the lake?
audioscript.speaker: VISITOR

audioscript.text: Well, what you can do is take a bike over on the ship, and then go on a cycling trip.

audioscript.text: There's a trail there called the Back Road.
audioscript.speaker: TC EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: You could easily spend three or four hours exploring it, and the scenery's wonderful.
audioscript.speaker: TC EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: They'll give you a map when you get your ticket for the cruise, there's no extra charge.

audioscript.text: I'll just make a note of that.

audioscript.text: Uh. How do you spell it?
audioscript.speaker: VISITOR

audioscript.text: RATCHESONS.
audioscript.speaker: TC EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: It's just by the cruise ship terminal.
audioscript.speaker: TC EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: OK.
audioscript.speaker: VISITOR

audioscript.text: Fine, that shouldn't be a problem.

audioscript.speaker: VISITOR

audioscript.text: Sure, you should definitely get that.

audioscript.speaker: TC EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: You won't see any shops round there or anywhere to stay, so you need to get back in time for the last boat.
audioscript.speaker: TC EMPLOYEE
audioscript.explain: Q9: The passage warns *'you won't see any shops round there or anywhere to stay'*. So there are no **shops** or accommodation in the area.

audioscript.text: Yeah.
audioscript.speaker: VISITOR

audioscript.text: Uh. So what sort of prices are we looking at here?
audioscript.speaker: VISITOR

audioscript.text: Let's see, that would be one adult and one child for the cruise with Farm tour.
audioscript.speaker: TC EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: That's 117 dollars, and an adult and a child for the cruise only, so that's $214 altogether.
audioscript.speaker: TC EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: Oh, wait a minute.
audioscript.speaker: TC EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: How old did you say your daughter was?
audioscript.speaker: TC EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: Then I'm afraid it's $267, because she has to pay the adult fare, which is $75, instead of the child fare, which is $22 sorry about that.
audioscript.speaker: TC EMPLOYEE

audioscript.text: That's OK.
audioscript.speaker: VISITOR

audioscript.text: Er, so how do...
audioscript.speaker: VISITOR

audioscript.text: That is the end of section 1.

audioscript.text: Good morning everyone.
audioscript.speaker: JOY PARKINS

audioscript.text: My name's Joy Parkins, and I'm the restaurant manager.
audioscript.speaker: JOY PARKINS

audioscript.text: And I understand that none of you've had any previous experience as kitchen assistants.
audioscript.speaker: JOY PARKINS

audioscript.text: Well, you might be feeling a bit nervous now, but most of our kitchen assistants say they enjoy the work.
audioscript.speaker: JOY PARKINS

audioscript.text: OK, they might get shouted at sometimes, but it's nothing personal.
audioscript.speaker: JOY PARKINS

audioscript.text: And they're pleased that they have so many different things to do, which means they never get bored.
audioscript.speaker: JOY PARKINS
audioscript.explain: Q11: The manager says staff are pleased they have *'so many different things to do'* — **'different things'** means **'variety'**. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: And I'll tell you straight away that if you do well, we might think about moving you up and giving you some more responsibility.
audioscript.speaker: JOY PARKINS

audioscript.text: Right, well, you've all shown up on time, which is an excellent start.
audioscript.speaker: JOY PARKINS

audioscript.text: Now I'm glad to see none of you have unsuitable footwear, so that's good.
audioscript.speaker: JOY PARKINS

audioscript.text: You need to be careful as the floors can get very wet and slippery.
audioscript.speaker: JOY PARKINS

audioscript.text: Those of you with long hair have got it well out of the way, but some of you'll need to remove your rings and bracelets, just put them somewhere safe for today.
audioscript.speaker: JOY PARKINS
audioscript.explain: Q12: The manager says some staff *'need to remove your rings and bracelets'* — **'rings and bracelets'** are **'jewellery'**. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: And remember to leave them at home tomorrow, as they can be a safety hazard.
audioscript.speaker: JOY PARKINS

audioscript.text: Now it's going to be a busy day for you all today.
audioscript.speaker: JOY PARKINS

audioscript.text: We don't have any tables free for this evening.

audioscript.text: Section 3.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear two students called Trudie and Stewart, who are both studying to be librarians, discussing a paper that they are going to write together.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 23.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 23.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: OK, Stewart, we need to start planning our paper on public libraries.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Have you thought of an angle yet?
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Well, there's so much we could look into, how libraries have changed over the centuries, for instance, or how different countries organize them, what do you think, Trudie?
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: Maybe we should concentrate on this country and try to relate the changes in libraries to external developments, like the fact that far more people can read than a century ago, and that the local population may speak lots of different languages.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE
audioscript.explain: Q21: Trudie says they should *'concentrate on this country'* and *'relate the changes in libraries to external developments'* — **'external developments'** means **'changes in society'**. So the main topic is how changes in society are reflected in public libraries. The answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: We could include something about changes in the source of funding too.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: Yes, but remember we're only supposed to write a short paper, so it's probably best if we don't go into funding in any detail.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Right, well, shall we just brainstorm a few ideas to get started?
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: OK, we obviously need to look at the impact of new technology, particularly the internet.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Now that lots of books have been digitalized, people can access them from their own computers at home.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: And if everyone did that, libraries would be obsolete.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: Yes.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: But the digitalized books that are available online for free are mostly out of copyright, aren't they?
audioscript.speaker: STEWART
audioscript.explain: Q22: Stewart says free digitalized books are *'mostly out of copyright'* — **'out of copyright'** means they are **old**. He adds you won't find the *'latest best-seller or up-to-date information'*. So the disadvantage is that they are generally old. The answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: And copyright in this country lasts for 70 years after the author dies.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: So you won't find the latest best-seller or up-to-date information.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART
audioscript.explain: Q22: Stewart says free digitalized books are *'mostly out of copyright'* — **'out of copyright'** means they are **old**. He adds you won't find the *'latest best-seller or up-to-date information'*. So the disadvantage is that they are generally old. The answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: That's an important point.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Anyway, I find it hard to concentrate when I'm reading a long text on a screen.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: I'd much rather read a physical book, and it takes longer to read on a screen.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Oh, I prefer it.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: I suppose it's just a personal preference.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: Hmm, I expect libraries will go on evolving in the next few years.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Some have already become centers where community activities take place.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Like local clubs meeting there, I think that'll become even more common.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: I'd like to think so, and that they'll still be serving their traditional function, but I'm not so sure.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: There are financial implications after all.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: What I'm afraid will happen is that books and magazines will all disappear, and there'll just be rows and rows of computers.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART
audioscript.explain: Q23: Stewart says he's afraid that *'books and magazines will all disappear, and there'll just be rows and rows of computers'*. This means he expects libraries will no longer contain any books. The answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: They won't look anything like the libraries we're used to.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: Well, we'll see.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 24 to 30.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 24 to 30.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: I've just had an idea.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Why don't we make an in-depth study of our local public library as background to our paper?
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Yes, that'd be interesting, and raise all sorts of issues.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: Let's make a list of possible things we could ask about, then work out some sort of structure.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: For instance, um, we could interview some of the staff, and find out whether the library has its own budget, or if that's controlled by the local council.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART
audioscript.explain: Q24: The passage says they want to find out *'whether the library has its own budget'*. The question asks if it has a **budget** of its own. So the answer is **'budget'**.

audioscript.text: And what their policies are.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: I know they don't allow food, but I'd love to find out what types of noise they ban.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: There always seems to be a lot of talking, but never music.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Hmm, I don't know if that's a policy or it just happens.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Ah. I've often wondered.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: Then there are things like how the library is affected by employment laws.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART
audioscript.explain: Q25: The passage mentions *'how the library is affected by employment laws'*. The question asks about laws regarding all aspects of **employment**. So the answer is **'employment'**.

audioscript.text: I suppose there are rules about working hours, facilities for staff and so on.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Then there are other issues relating to the design of the building and how customers use it, like what measures does the library take to ensure their safety?

audioscript.explain: Q26: The passage asks *'what measures does the library take to ensure their safety?'* The question says the design needs to take the **safety** of customers into account. So the answer is **'safety'**.

audioscript.text: They'd need floor coverings that aren't slippery,
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: and emergency exits for instance.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Oh, and another thing, there's the question of the kind of insurance the library needs to have, in case anyone gets injured.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE
audioscript.explain: Q27: The passage talks about *'the kind of insurance the library needs to have, in case anyone gets injured'*. The question asks what **insurance** is required in case of accidents. So the answer is **'insurance'**.

audioscript.text: Yes, that's something else to find out.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: You know something I've often wondered.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: What's that?
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Well, you know they've got an archive of local newspapers going back years.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: Well, next to it, they've got the diary of a well known politician from the late 19th century.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART
audioscript.explain: Q28: The passage says they have *'the diary of a well known politician'*. The question asks why a famous person's **diary** is located in the library. So the answer is **'diary'**.

audioscript.text: I wonder why it's there.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: Do you know what his connection was with this area?
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: No idea.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Let's add it to our list of things to find out.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Oh, I've just thought - you know people might ask in the library about local organizations, like sports clubs?
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE

audioscript.text: Hmm. Well, I wonder if they keep a database, or whether they just look online.
audioscript.speaker: TRUDIE
audioscript.explain: Q29: The passage wonders *'if they keep a database'* of local organizations. The question asks whether it has a **database** of local organisations. So the answer is **'database'**.

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: I quite fancy finding out what the differences are between a library that's open to the public and one that's part of a museum, for example.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART
audioscript.explain: Q30: The passage wants to find differences between a public library and one that's *'part of a museum'*. The question asks how it's different from a library in a **museum**. So the answer is **'museum'**.

audioscript.text: They must be very different.
audioscript.speaker: STEWART

audioscript.text: Hmm, then something else I'd like to know is...

utterances.text: You will hear two students called Trudie and Stewart, who are both studying to be librarians, discussing a paper that they are going to write together.
utterances.speaker: ANNOUNCER

utterances.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 23.
utterances.speaker: ANNOUNCER

utterances.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 23.
utterances.speaker: ANNOUNCER

utterances.text: OK, Stewart, we need to start planning our paper on public libraries.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Have you thought of an angle yet?
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Well, there's so much we could look into, how libraries have changed over the centuries, for instance, or how different countries organize them, what do you think, Trudie?
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: Maybe we should concentrate on this country and try to relate the changes in libraries to external developments, like the fact that far more people can read than a century ago, and that the local population may speak lots of different languages.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE
utterances.explain: Q21: Trudie says they should *'concentrate on this country'* and *'relate the changes in libraries to external developments'* — **'external developments'** means **'changes in society'**. So the main topic is how changes in society are reflected in public libraries. The answer is **B**.

utterances.text: We could include something about changes in the source of funding too.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: Yes, but remember we're only supposed to write a short paper, so it's probably best if we don't go into funding in any detail.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Right, well, shall we just brainstorm a few ideas to get started?
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: OK, we obviously need to look at the impact of new technology, particularly the internet.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Now that lots of books have been digitalized, people can access them from their own computers at home.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: And if everyone did that, libraries would be obsolete.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: Yes.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: But the digitalized books that are available online for free are mostly out of copyright, aren't they?
utterances.speaker: STEWART
utterances.explain: Q22: Stewart says free digitalized books are *'mostly out of copyright'* — **'out of copyright'** means they are **old**. He adds you won't find the *'latest best-seller or up-to-date information'*. So the disadvantage is that they are generally old. The answer is **C**.

utterances.text: And copyright in this country lasts for 70 years after the author dies.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: So you won't find the latest best-seller or up-to-date information.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: That's an important point.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Anyway, I find it hard to concentrate when I'm reading a long text on a screen.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: I'd much rather read a physical book, and it takes longer to read on a screen.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Oh, I prefer it.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: I suppose it's just a personal preference.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: Hmm, I expect libraries will go on evolving in the next few years.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Some have already become centers where community activities take place.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Like local clubs meeting there, I think that'll become even more common.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: I'd like to think so, and that they'll still be serving their traditional function, but I'm not so sure.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: There are financial implications after all.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: What I'm afraid will happen is that books and magazines will all disappear, and there'll just be rows and rows of computers.

utterances.text: They won't look anything like the libraries we're used to.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: Well, we'll see.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 24 to 30.
utterances.speaker: ANNOUNCER

utterances.text: I've just had an idea.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Why don't we make an in-depth study of our local public library as background to our paper?
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Yes, that'd be interesting, and raise all sorts of issues.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: Let's make a list of possible things we could ask about, then work out some sort of structure.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: For instance, um, we could interview some of the staff, and find out whether the library has its own budget, or if that's controlled by the local council.
utterances.speaker: STEWART
utterances.explain: Q24: The passage says they want to find out *'whether the library has its own budget'*. The question asks if it has a **budget** of its own. So the answer is **'budget'**.

utterances.text: And what their policies are.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: I know they don't allow food, but I'd love to find out what types of noise they ban.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: There always seems to be a lot of talking, but never music.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Hmm, I don't know if that's a policy or it just happens.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Ah. I've often wondered.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: Then there are things like how the library is affected by employment laws.
utterances.speaker: STEWART
utterances.explain: Q25: The passage mentions *'how the library is affected by employment laws'*. The question asks about laws regarding all aspects of **employment**. So the answer is **'employment'**.

utterances.text: I suppose there are rules about working hours, facilities for staff and so on.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: Right.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Then there are other issues relating to the design of the building and how customers use it, like what measures does the library take to ensure their safety?
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE
utterances.explain: Q26: The passage asks *'what measures does the library take to ensure their safety?'* The question says the design needs to take the **safety** of customers into account. So the answer is **'safety'**.

utterances.text: They'd need floor coverings that aren't slippery,
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: and emergency exits for instance.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Oh, and another thing, there's the question of the kind of insurance the library needs to have, in case anyone gets injured.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE
utterances.explain: Q27: The passage talks about *'the kind of insurance the library needs to have, in case anyone gets injured'*. The question asks what **insurance** is required in case of accidents. So the answer is **'insurance'**.

utterances.text: Yes, that's something else to find out.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: You know something I've often wondered.

utterances.text: What's that?
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Well, you know they've got an archive of local newspapers going back years.

utterances.text: Well, next to it, they've got the diary of a well known politician from the late 19th century.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: I wonder why it's there.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: Do you know what his connection was with this area?
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: No idea.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Let's add it to our list of things to find out.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Oh, I've just thought - you know people might ask in the library about local organizations, like sports clubs?
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Hmm. Well, I wonder if they keep a database, or whether they just look online.
utterances.speaker: TRUDIE

utterances.text: Right.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: I quite fancy finding out what the differences are between a library that's open to the public and one that's part of a museum, for example.
utterances.speaker: STEWART

utterances.text: They must be very different.

body.title: Four business values

audioscript.text: Section 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear part of a lecture for business students about business values.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: In public discussion of business, we take certain values for granted.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Today, I'm going to talk about four of them.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Collaboration, hard work, creativity, and excellence.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Uh. Most people would say they're all good things.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I'm going to suggest that's an over-simple view.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The trouble with these values is that they're theoretical concepts removed from the reality of day-to-day business, uh, pursue values by all means.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But be prepared for what may happen as a result.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They can actually cause damage, which is not at all the intention.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says business values *'can actually cause damage'* — the question asks what many business values can result in. **'Result in'** means the same as **'cause'**. So the answer is **damage**.

audioscript.text: Business leaders generally try to do the right thing, but all too often the right thing backfires.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: If those leaders adopt values without understanding and managing the side effects that arise.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage warns that leaders adopt values *'without understanding and managing the side effects that arise'* — the question says managers need to deal with the potential something. **'Deal with'** matches **'managing'**. So the answer is **side effects**.

audioscript.text: The values can easily get in the way of what's actually intended.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: OK, so the first value I'm going to discuss is collaboration.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Uh. Let me give you an example, on a management training course I once attended.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We were put into groups, and had to construct a bridge across a stream, using building blocks that we were given.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage describes the training task: *'had to construct a bridge across a stream'* — the question asks what the team had to build. **'Construct'** means **'build'**. So the answer is **bridge**.

audioscript.text: The rule was that everyone in the team had to move at least one building block during the construction.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This was intended to encourage teamwork, but it was really a job best done by one person.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The other teams tried to collaborate on building the structure, and descended into confusion with everyone getting in each other's way.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says other teams *'descended into confusion'* when they tried to collaborate — the question asks what other teams experienced. **'Experienced'** matches what they *'descended into'*. So the answer is **confusion**.

audioscript.text: Our team leader solved the challenge brilliantly.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: She simply asked everyone in the team to move a piece a few centimeters to comply with the rule, and then let the person in the team with an aptitude for puzzles like this build it alone.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We finished before any other team.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: My point is that the task wasn't really suited to team working, so why make it one?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Teamwork can also lead to inconsistency, a common cause of poor sales.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In the case of a smartphone that a certain company launched.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage gives an example of poor sales: *'In the case of a smartphone that a certain company launched'* — the question asks what product had poor sales. The passage directly names the product. So the answer is **smartphone**.

audioscript.text: One director wanted to target the business market, and another demanded it was aimed at consumers.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The company wanted both directors to be involved.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So gave the product a consumer-friendly name, but marketed it to companies.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The result was that it met the needs of neither group.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It would have been better to let one director or the other have his way, not both.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Now industriousness or hard work.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's easy to mock people who say they work hard.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Uh. After all, a hamster running around in a wheel is working hard, and getting nowhere.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Of course, hard work is valuable, but only when properly targeted, otherwise it wastes the resources that companies value most, time and energy.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says hard work *'wastes the resources that companies value most'* — the question says hard work may be a bad use of company something. **'Bad use'** matches **'wastes'**. So the answer is **resources**.

audioscript.text: And that's bad for the organization.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: There's a management model that groups people according to four criteria, clever, hard-working, stupid, and lazy.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Here, lazy means having a rational determination not to carry out unnecessary tasks.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage defines lazy as *'not to carry out unnecessary tasks'* — the question asks what tasks lazy people avoid. **'Avoid doing'** matches **'not to carry out'**. So the answer is **unnecessary**.

audioscript.text: It doesn't mean trying to avoid work altogether.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Most people display two of these characteristics, and the most valuable people are those who are both clever and lazy.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They possess intellectual clarity.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And they don't rush into making decisions.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They come up with solutions to save the time and energy spent by the stupid and hard-working group.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Instead of throwing more man hours at a problem, the clever and lazy group looks for a more effective solution.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Next, we come to creativity.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This often works well, creating an attention grabbing TV commercial for example, might lead to increased sales.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But it isn't always a good thing.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Some advertising campaigns are remembered for their creativity without having any effect on sales.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This happened a few years ago with the launch of a chocolate bar.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage mentions a failed campaign: *'with the launch of a chocolate bar'* — the question asks what product the campaign was for. The passage directly names the product. So the answer is **chocolate bar**.

audioscript.text: Subsequent research showed that plenty of consumers remembered the adverts, but had no idea what was being advertised.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The trouble is that the creator derives pleasure from coming up with the idea.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And wrongly assumes the audience for the campaign will share that feeling.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A company that brings out thousands of new products may seem more creative than a company that only has a few, but it may be too creative.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And make smaller profits.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Creativity needs to be targeted to solve a problem that the company has identified.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says creativity should *'solve a problem that the company has identified'* — the question says creativity should respond to a particular something. **'Respond to'** matches **'solve'**. So the answer is **problem**.

audioscript.text: Just coming up with more and more novel products isn't necessarily a good thing.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And finally, excellence.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We all know companies that claim they strive for excellence, but it takes a long time to achieve excellence.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In business, being first with a product is more profitable than having the best product.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A major study of company performance compared pioneers - that is, companies bringing out the first version of a particular product - with followers, the companies that copied and improved on that product.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The study found that the pioneers commanded an average market share of 29 percent, while the followers achieved less than half that.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says pioneers *'commanded an average market share of 29 percent'* — the question asks what pioneers had that was far higher than followers. The passage directly compares this number. So the answer is **market share**.

audioscript.text: Only 13 percent, even though their product might have been better.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Insisting on excellence in everything we do is time consuming, wastes energy, and leads to losing out on opportunities.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Sometimes, second-rate work is more worthwhile than excellence.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: 'Make sure it's excellent' sounds like a good approach to business.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But the just get started approach is likely to be more successful.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is the end of Section 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Yes.

audioscript.text: And the display takes place on the opposite side of the river.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Sounds great.

audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Where is that being held?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Lovely.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: I'm interested in all kinds of dancing, so I'm sure I'll enjoy that.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Hmm, I'm sure you will.

audioscript.text: Yes, you can book online.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Or you can buy them when you arrive in Kenton, either at the festival box office or from any shops displaying our logo in the windows.
audioscript.speaker: MAN
audioscript.explain: Q10: The passage says you can buy tickets from shops *'displaying our logo in the windows'* — so the shops show the festival **logo**. So the answer is **logo**.

audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Thank you so much for all your help.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: You're welcome.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: I hope you enjoy your stay.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Thank you.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Goodbye.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Right, I've now almost succeeded in finalizing plans for our tour, so I'll bring you up to date with what I know.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As you know, we're flying first to Munich on Monday the 4th.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The flight is at 11:30 so it's too early to have lunch at the airport.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I suggest we meet there for coffee at 10, which should give us plenty of time for breakfast before we leave home.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q11: The speaker says *'I suggest we meet there for coffee at 10'* — so they will have **coffee** at the airport. He also says they will have *'breakfast before we leave home'*, not at the airport. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: When we arrive in Munich, we'll be met at the airport by Claus Bauer.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Claus works for a tour operator, and he'll look after us for the time we'll be in Germany.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q12: The passage says *'Claus works for a tour operator, and he'll look after us'* — so Claus is a **tour operator** employee. ***Don't be tricked by 'an officer of the National Theatre'*** — that person gives a tour later, but does not meet them at the airport. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: He's already liaised with the managers of the theatres we're going to visit, and he's also arranged for an officer of the National Theatre in Munich to show us round the theater one afternoon during our stay.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Now last time we discussed this trip, I didn't have the precise cost for hotel rooms, but now I have.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The normal rate at the hotel where we're staying is €150 a night for a double room.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I'd hoped to get that down to 120 euros, but in fact I've been able to negotiate a rate of 110.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q13: The speaker says the normal rate is *'€150'*, he hoped for *'120 euros'*, but he actually got *'a rate of 110'*. So the final price they pay is **110 euros**. The answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: That'll be reflected in the final payment which you'll need to make by the end of this week.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: On Tuesday, the day after our arrival, I had hoped we could sit in on a rehearsal at one of the theaters, but unfortunately that's proved very difficult to arrange.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So instead, we'll have a coach trip to one of the amazing castles in the mountains south of Munich.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: On Tuesday evening, we'll all have dinner together in a restaurant near our hotel, from talking to you all about your preferences.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It was clear that a typical local restaurant would be too meat oriented for some of you.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Some of you suggested an Italian restaurant.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But I must confess that I decided to book a Lebanese one, as we have plenty of opportunities to go to an Italian restaurant at home.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q14: The speaker says *'I decided to book a Lebanese one'* — **'one'** means **'restaurant'**. He mentions an Italian restaurant was suggested, but he chose the **Lebanese** one instead. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: On Wednesday afternoon, the director of the play we're going to see that evening will talk to us at the theater.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q15: The passage says *'the director of the play... will talk to us at the theater'* on Wednesday afternoon. So they will meet a **theatre director**. The answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: She'll describe the whole process of producing a play.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Including how she chose the actors, and as the play we're going to see is a modern one, how she worked with the playwright.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Right, now I'd just like to make a few points about the plays we're going to see, partly because it might influence your choice of clothes to take with you.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The play we're seeing on Wednesday evening is a modern one, and we're going to the premiere.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q16: The passage says Wednesday's play is *'the premiere'* — **'premiere'** means the **first time** a play is performed. So the correct comment is **F**.

audioscript.text: So it'll be quite a dressy occasion, though of course you don't have to dress formally.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I gather it's rather a multimedia production with amazing lighting effects and a soundtrack of electronic music, though unfortunately the playwright is ill and is unlikely to be able to attend.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: On Thursday, we're seeing a play that was first performed last year, when it was commissioned to mark a hundred years since the birth in the town of a well-known scientist.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q17: The passage says Thursday's play was *'commissioned to mark a hundred years since the birth... of a well-known scientist'* — this means it was written to **celebrate an anniversary**. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: We're going to see a revival of that production, which aroused a lot of interest.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Friday's play will really make you think hard about what clothes to pack, as it'll be in the garden of a palace.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q18: The passage says Friday's play will be *'in the garden of a palace'* — a garden is **outdoors**. So the play will be **performed outdoors**, which matches comment **E**.

audioscript.text: It's a beautiful setting.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But I'd better warn you, there won't be much protection from the wind.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: On Saturday, we're going by coach to a theater in another town, not far from Munich.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This will be the opening of a drama festival.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And the mayor and all the other dignitaries of the town will be attending.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q19: The passage says on Saturday *'the mayor and all the other dignitaries of the town will be attending'* — **'dignitaries'** means important **officials**. So the performance will be **attended by officials from the town**, which is comment **G**.

audioscript.text: After the performance, the mayor is hosting a reception for all the audience.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And there'll be a band playing traditional music of the region.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: After having a day off on Sunday, our final play is on Monday, and it's in the stunning setting of the Old Town Hall, which dates back to the 14th century.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q20: The passage says Monday's play is in the *'Old Town Hall, which dates back to the 14th century'* — a 14th-century town hall is a **historic building**. So the play will be **performed inside a historic building**, matching comment **C**.

audioscript.text: The performance marks the fifty years that the lead actor has been on stage, and the play is the one where he made his first professional appearance, all those years ago.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And the day after that, we'll be flying back home.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Now, have you got any questions before I...
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is the end of section 2.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Section 3.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear James, who is in the Scandinavian Studies department at his university, talking to his tutor Beth.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Oh, good morning.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: Uh, You must be James.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: I'm Beth Cartwright.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: Please call me Beth.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: Thank you.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: Now as this is your first tutorial since you started on the Scandinavian Studies course.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: I'd like to find out something about you.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: Why did you decide to take this course?
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: Well, my mother is Danish, and although we always lived in England.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: She used to talk about her home a lot, and that made me want to visit Denmark.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: We hardly ever did though, my mother usually went on her own.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: But whenever her relations or friends were in England, they always came to see us.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES
audioscript.explain: Q21: The question asks why James chose this course as a child. The passage says *'whenever her relations or friends were in England, they always came to see us'* — this means many Danish people visited his family. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: I see.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: So I assume you already speak Danish, one of the languages you'll be studying.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: I can get by when I talk to people, though I'm not terribly accurate.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: Now you probably know that you'll spend the third year of the course abroad.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: Have you had any thoughts about that?
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: I'm really looking forward to it.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: And although Denmark seems the obvious place to go, because of my family connections, I'd love to spend the time in Iceland.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: Oh, I'm sure it can be arranged.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: Do you have any plans for when you graduate?
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: A lot of students go on to take a master's degree.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: I think the 4 years of the undergraduate course will be enough for me.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: I'm interested in journalism, and I quite like the idea of moving to Scandinavia and writing for magazines.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES
audioscript.explain: Q22: The question asks about James's plan after graduation. He says *'I'm interested in journalism... writing for magazines'* — **'journalism'** and **'magazines'** are part of the **media**. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: I'd find that more creative than translating.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: Which I suppose most graduates do.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: OK, now how are you finding the courses you're taking this term, James?
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: Well, I'm really enjoying the one on Swedish cinema.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: That'll continue next term, but the one on Scandinavian literature that's running at the moment will be replaced by more specialized courses.
audioscript.speaker: BETH
audioscript.explain: Q23: The question asks which course ends this term. The passage says the course on *'Scandinavian literature that's running at the moment will be replaced'* — **'running at the moment'** means it is happening now, and **'replaced'** means it will end. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: Oh, and by the way.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: If you're interested in watching Danish television programs, there's going to be a course on that the term after next.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: That sounds good.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: Have you started thinking about the literature paper that you have to write in the next few weeks?
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: Yes, my first choice would be to do something on the Icelandic sagas.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: Hmm, the trouble with that is that a lot of people choose that topic, and it can be difficult to get hold of the books you'll need.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: Why not leave that for another time?
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: You might find modern novels or 19th century playwrights interesting.
audioscript.speaker: BETH
audioscript.explain: Q24: The question asks about the topic of James's literature paper. Beth suggests *'19th century playwrights'*, and James agrees, saying *'that would be a good idea'*. ***The Icelandic sagas were his first choice, but Beth said to leave that for another time***. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: I've read or seen several plays in translation, so that would be a good idea.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES
audioscript.explain: Q24: The question asks about the topic of James's literature paper. Beth suggests *'19th century playwrights'*, and James agrees, saying *'that would be a good idea'*. ***The Icelandic sagas were his first choice, but Beth said to leave that for another time***. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: Fine, I'll put you down for that topic.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: Right, so what would you advise me to aim at in the paper?
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: First, I suggest you avoid taking one writer and going into a great deal of detail.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: That approach certainly has its place, but I think you first need to get an understanding of the literature in the context of the society in which it was produced, who it was written for.
audioscript.speaker: BETH
audioscript.explain: Q25: The question asks what Beth recommends for the paper. She says to understand literature *'in the context of the society in which it was produced'* — this means the **social background**. She also says this is better than focusing on one writer or the history of the genre. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: How it was published and so on.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: I also think that's more fruitful than placing it within the history of the genre.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: OK, that sounds reasonable.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Could I ask for some advice about writing the paper I'm working on about the Vikings?
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: I have to do that this week, and I'm a bit stuck.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: Of course.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: Have you decided yet what to write about?
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: No, I haven't.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: There's so much that seems interesting, Viking settlement in other countries, trade, mythology.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: Well, what I suggest is that you read an assignment a student wrote last year, which is kept in the library.
audioscript.speaker: BETH
audioscript.explain: Q26: The question asks what James will read first. Beth suggests he read *'an assignment a student wrote last year'* — an **'assignment'** is a **student paper**. So the answer is **E**.

audioscript.text: It's short and well focused, and I'm sure you'll find it helpful.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: I'll give you the details in a moment.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: Textbooks usually cover so many topics, it can be very difficult to choose just one.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: OK.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: I've got a DVD of the film about the Vikings that came out earlier this year.
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: Should I watch that again?
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: If it's the one I am thinking of... I'd ignore it.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: It's more fantasy than reality, but I've got a recording of a documentary that you should watch.
audioscript.speaker: BETH
audioscript.explain: Q27: The question asks what James will borrow from Beth. She says *'I've got a recording of a documentary that you should watch'* — a **'recording'** is something you can borrow. So the answer is **G**.

audioscript.text: It makes some interesting and provocative points, which I think will help you to focus your topic.
audioscript.speaker: BETH

audioscript.text: Right, so then should I work out an outline?
audioscript.speaker: JAMES

audioscript.text: Yes, just headings for different sections at this stage, and then you should start looking for suitable articles and books to draw on.
audioscript.speaker: BETH
audioscript.explain: Q28: The question asks what James will plan next. Beth says to make *'headings for different sections'* — **'headings'** and **'sections'** create the paper's **structure**. So the answer is **D**.

audioscript.text: And take notes which you organize according to those headings.
audioscript.speaker: BETH
audioscript.explain: Q29: The question asks what James will write after reading. Beth tells him to *'take notes which you organize according to those headings'* — so he will write **notes**. So the answer is **C**.

body.title: Conflict at work

audioscript.text: Section 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about conflict at work, given by a business studies lecturer.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Over the years, attitudes towards workers have changed considerably.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: After all, there was a time when workers had no rights at all.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And labored in appalling conditions.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Conditions have improved a lot, but conflict in the workplace is still common.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And human resources managers nowadays need to be able to deal with it when necessary.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: What is conflict in the workplace?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Definitions vary, but I'm taking it to refer to a whole range of behaviors that the victim finds unacceptable.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: From minor, harmless arguments to - at the opposite extreme - physical violence.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Much of this is covered by the term bullying.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says *'Much of this is covered by the term bullying'* — **'this'** refers to the whole range of conflict behaviors just described. So the general category is **bullying**.

audioscript.text: By which I mean one or more people behaving abusively or aggressively against another who is in a weaker position.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Although all behavior like this is a form of conflict, not all conflict can be described in these terms.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As with all human behavior, there are numerous reasons for it, but often it's caused by someone who feels the need to show their superiority over someone else, in order to feel that they aren't at the lowest level in a hierarchy or a group of people.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says conflict is often caused by someone who feels the need to *'show their superiority over someone else'* — **'show their superiority'** means to prove they are better. So the answer is **superiority**.

audioscript.text: In some cases, one person simply dislikes the other, on the basis that the personality of one is in some way incompatible with that of the other person.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says one person may dislike another because *'the personality of one is in some way incompatible with that of the other person'* — **'incompatible'** means they do not match, so the difference is in **personality**.

audioscript.text: A general habit of optimism in one person could make them intolerant of a colleague who's constantly pessimistic - not that that justifies treating them badly, of course.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Some conflicts arise when people are more interested in promoting themselves and their team than in the company as a whole.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: These conflicts are called 'structural', and could come about, for example, when a sales team believe they are the only people in the business who do any useful work, and look down on behind-the-scenes administrators.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says *'These conflicts are called 'structural''* — **'these'** points back to conflicts where people promote their own team over the company. So the answer is **structural**.

audioscript.text: Conflict obviously affects the individuals concerned - the situation is likely to be very stressful for victims, resulting in their absence from work, possibly for months.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says stress for victims results in *'their absence from work, possibly for months'* — **'absence'** means not being there. So the answer is **absence**.

audioscript.text: For the company, if no effort is made to deal with conflict, it can spiral out of control, and even lead to the breakdown of the business.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Some interesting work with chief executives - CEOs - has uncovered some of the reasons why they may treat colleagues badly.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Many CEOs combine two opposing characteristics: confidence - that is, the belief that they're capable of great achievements - with a high level of anxiety, a fear of missing targets, whether set by themselves or by the directors of the company.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says many CEOs combine two opposing characteristics: *'confidence... with a high level of anxiety'* — **'confidence'** is the first one mentioned. So the answer is **confidence**.

audioscript.text: This combination can make them respond badly to anyone who questions their decisions.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In a high pressure work environment, such characteristics become problematic, and it's particularly difficult to tackle the situation where colleagues, managers, and board members are all trying to achieve their own visions.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says problems arise when colleagues, managers, and board members are all trying to achieve *'their own visions'* — **'visions'** means their own ideas about where the business should go. So the answer is **visions**.

audioscript.text: When they can't agree on strategic issues, and on where they see the business going, there are real problems.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For managers at lower levels within the organization, it might seem that an autocratic form of management - where the chief executive gives orders and everyone else has to obey - would see more conflict than others.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Interestingly though, a company with a more democratic business model can suffer more when uncertainty about who to report to leads to conflicting demands.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says a company with a more *'democratic business model'* can suffer from uncertainty about who to report to — **'democratic'** is the structure that creates this problem. So the answer is **democratic**.

audioscript.text: Now I'll say a little about dealing with the type of conflict that has harmful effects.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Of course, the ideal is to prevent it arising in the first place.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A good manager at any level will make efforts to earn the respect of the people they work with, particularly those who report to them.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says a good manager will make efforts to *'earn the respect'* of the people they work with — **'earn'** means to try hard to gain. So the answer is **respect**.

audioscript.text: That will involve politeness in all communications, and treating them as equals who happen to have a different role within the organization.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Sometimes, of course, conflict does occur, and can get out of hand.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In such cases, the human resources department often gets involved.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: However, if one of the parties in a conflict sees human resources as simply a mouthpiece for the chief executive, then an external mediator might be able to help. By talking to both sides and trying to find the truth of what's been happening.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says if human resources is seen as just a mouthpiece, then an *'external mediator'* might be able to help — **'external'** means from outside the company. So the answer is **mediator**.

audioscript.text: They can build a clear picture of the situation, and give feedback that both sides will accept, precisely because they're independent.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is the end of Section 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: Hi, Susie, it's Paul here.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: How are you?
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Enjoying your new job?
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: You're working at the library, aren't you?
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Yes, I started when the library reopened a month ago.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: It's great.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: Actually, Carol and I have been meaning to join for a while.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Oh, you should.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: It doesn't cost anything, and the new library has all sorts of facilities.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: It's not just a place where you borrow books.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: For instance, there's an area with comfortable seats where you can sit and read the magazines they have there.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: Some people spend the whole morning there.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: Hmm, wish I had that amount of time to spend.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Yes, you must be pretty busy at present, with the children and everything.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: We are, yes, but we're hoping to get away this summer.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: We're thinking of going to Greece.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Well, we've got a much larger section of the library devoted to travel books now.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE
audioscript.explain: Q1: The passage says the library has *'a much larger section... devoted to travel books now'* — **'travel books'** means books about **'travel'**. So the answer is **travel**.

audioscript.text: So you should come and have a look.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: I can't remember if there's anything specifically on Greece, but I should think so.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: OK.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Now Carol's organizing a project for the history class she teaches at school.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: It's about life in the town 100 years ago.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Do you have anything that might be useful?
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Yes, actually we've now got a new section with materials on the history of the town and surrounding region.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE
audioscript.explain: Q2: The passage says they have *'a new section with materials on the history of the town'* — **'history of the town'** is the same as **'local history'**. So the answer is **history**.

audioscript.text: Right, I'll tell her.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: You can't always find that sort of thing on the internet.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Now, in the old library, there used to be a separate room with reference books.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: It was a really nice quiet room.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Yes, we've put those books in the main part of the library now, but we do have a room called the community room.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: It can be hired out for meetings, but at other times, people can use it to study.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE
audioscript.explain: Q3: The passage says the community room can be hired for meetings, but *'at other times, people can use it to study'* — **'use it to'** means it is **'possible to'** do this. So the answer is **study**.

audioscript.text: I might use that.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: It's hard to find anywhere quiet at home sometimes.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: I can't remember how old your son and daughter are.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: We've introduced a special section of fiction written specially for teenagers, but they might be a bit young for that.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE
audioscript.explain: Q4: The passage says they introduced *'a special section of fiction written specially for teenagers'* — **'fiction'** is a type of **'books'**. So the answer is **teenagers**.

audioscript.text: Yes, they would be.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 5 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 5 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Well, we do have lots of activities for younger children.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: Yes, for example, we have a science club.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: At the next meeting, they're going to be doing experiments with stuff that everyone has in the kitchen.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE
audioscript.explain: Q5: The passage says the experiments use *'stuff that everyone has in the kitchen'* — **'stuff from your kitchen'** means things you find in your **'kitchen'**. So the answer is **kitchen**.

audioscript.text: Sugar and flour and so on.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: They might be interested.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Yes, and we have a competition for children called Reading Challenge.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: That doesn't begin until after the end of term.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: They have to read six books, and they get a certificate if they manage it.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: So that gives them something to do while they're on holiday,
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: instead of getting bored.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: That's the idea.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: And there's special activities for adults too.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: On Friday, we have a local author called Tanya Streep, who's going to be talking about her new novel.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: It's called 'Catch the Mouse', and she based the story on a crime that actually took place here years ago.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE
audioscript.explain: Q6: The passage says the author *'based the story on a crime that actually took place'* — **'based on a real'** event means the story comes from a real **'crime'**. So the answer is **crime**.

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: We're not free on Friday, but I'll look out for the book.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Now, this probably isn't for you, but we do have IT support available for members.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: We get quite a few older people coming along, who are wanting to get up to speed with computer technology.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: It's on Tuesday mornings, they don't need to make an appointment or anything.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE
audioscript.explain: Q7: The passage says for IT support, *'they don't need to make an appointment or anything'* — **'no appointment is necessary'** means you do not need an **'appointment'**. So the answer is **appointment**.

audioscript.text: They just turn up.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: Well, my mother might be interested.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: I'll let her know.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: OK, and there's another service which you wouldn't expect from a library, which is a free medical check-up.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: The hospital arranges for someone to come along and measure the level of sugar in your blood, and they check cholesterol levels at the same time.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE
audioscript.explain: Q8: The passage says they *'measure the level of sugar in your blood'* — **'check of blood'** means they check the **'sugar'** in your blood. So the answer is **sugar**.

audioscript.text: Really?
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Yes, but that's only for the over 60s, so you wouldn't qualify.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: OK, well I'll tell my mother, she might be interested.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: What other information?
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE

audioscript.text: Well, we do have a little shop with things like wall charts and greetings cards, and also stamps, so you can post the card straight away, which is really useful.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE
audioscript.explain: Q9: The passage says the shop sells *'wall charts and greetings cards, and also stamps'* — **'stamps'** are sold there, so you can buy **'stamps'**. So the answer is **stamps**.

audioscript.text: Yeah.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Well, I'll bring the children round at the weekend, and we'll join.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Oh, one more thing, I'll be bringing the car.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Is there parking available?
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Yes, and it's free in the evening and at weekends.
audioscript.speaker: SUSIE
audioscript.explain: Q10: The passage says parking is *'free in the evening and at weekends'* — **'free parking'** means you do not pay for **'parking'**. So the answer is **parking**.

audioscript.text: Perfect.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: Well, thanks, Susie.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: See you soon.
audioscript.speaker: PAUL

audioscript.text: That is the end of section 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

audioscript.text: Section 2.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear part of a training session for new employees at a large travel company.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 17.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 17.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: In this session in your training day, we're going to look at some of the more specialized holidays we offer at BC Travel.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Now, the travel business is very competitive and it's important to be aware of how the market's changing and developing.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In terms of age groups, the over 65s are an important market, and one that's increasing steadily year on year.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain:
Q11: The passage says the over 65s are *'increasing steadily year on year'* — **'increasing'** means going up. It also says there is *'noticeable growth'* for the 55 to 64 year olds — **'growth'** also means going up. So the two age groups taking **increasing** numbers of holidays are **over 65 years** and **55-64 years**.

Q12: The passage says the over 65s are *'increasing steadily year on year'* — **'increasing'** means going up. It also says there is *'noticeable growth'* for the 55 to 64 year olds — **'growth'** also means going up. So the two age groups taking **increasing** numbers of holidays are **over 65 years** and **55-64 years**.

audioscript.text: The fewest holidays are taken by the 31 to 42 year olds.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And that figure shows no sign of rising.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The biggest market at present is still the youngest group, the 16 to 30s, but this group's also seen the biggest drop over the last few years.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Whereas there's a noticeable growth in the number of holidays taken by the 55 to 64 year olds.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain:
Q11: The passage says the over 65s are *'increasing steadily year on year'* — **'increasing'** means going up. It also says there is *'noticeable growth'* for the 55 to 64 year olds — **'growth'** also means going up. So the two age groups taking **increasing** numbers of holidays are **over 65 years** and **55-64 years**.

Q12: The passage says the over 65s are *'increasing steadily year on year'* — **'increasing'** means going up. It also says there is *'noticeable growth'* for the 55 to 64 year olds — **'growth'** also means going up. So the two age groups taking **increasing** numbers of holidays are **over 65 years** and **55-64 years**.

audioscript.text: As far as the 43 to 54 year olds are concerned, bookings there are steady, but I have to say we haven't seen the increase we expected.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One trend we're noticing with nearly all age groups is the growing popularity of holidays in which clients do some kind of specialized activity.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I'm not talking here about adventure holidays where clients take part in high risk activities like white water rafting, just for the thrill of it.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Activity holidays usually involve rather less high risk sports or things like art and music.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They're not necessarily cheaper than ordinary holidays, often the opposite in fact, but they do often take place outside the main tourist centers, which gives an opportunity for clients to find out more about the local people and customs.
