audioscript.text: Section 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear a lecturer on an environmental studies course discussing how birds are affected by environmental change.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: OK, so we've been looking at how manmade changes in our environment can affect wildlife.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Now, I'll discuss a particular example.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Let's take a look at mercury.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Mercury is one of the 120 or so elements.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That make up all matter, and it has the symbol Hg.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's a shiny silvery substance, you may have seen it in old-fashioned thermometers.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But it's not used much for domestic purposes now, because it's highly toxic.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But the problem is that the amount of mercury in the environment is increasing.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The main reason for this is the power plants used to produce electricity.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The main source of energy that most of them use is still coal, and when it's burned, it releases mercury into the atmosphere.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Some of this gets deposited into lakes and rivers, and if it's ingested by a fish, it's not excreted, it stays in the fish's body.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And it enters the food chain.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So, it's been known for some time that birds which eat fish may be affected, but what wasn't known until quite recently is that those that eat insects can also be affected.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says *'those that eat insects can also be affected'* — the question asks about birds which feed on something. **'feed on'** means **'eat'**. So the answer is **insects**.

audioscript.text: So, a woman called Claire Varian-Ramos is doing some research on how this is affecting birds.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And rather than looking at how many birds are actually killed by mercury poisoning, she's looking for more subtle sub-effects.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And these may be to do with the behavior of the birds, or with the effect of mercury on the way their brain works, so whether it leads to problems with memory for example.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says the effects may be to do with *'the behavior of the birds, or with the effect of mercury on the way their brain works'* — **'the way their brain works'** means **'mental processes'**. The question asks for effects on birds' something or mental processes. So the answer is **behaviour**.

audioscript.text: And she's particularly focusing on the effects of mercury on bird song.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Now, the process of song learning happens at a particular stage in the birds' development.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And what you may not know is that a young bird seems to acquire this skill by listening to the songs produced by its father, rather than by any other bird.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says a young bird learns song by listening to *'the songs produced by its father'* — the question says song is usually learned from a bird's something. So the answer is **father**.

audioscript.text: And Varian-Ramos has already found in her research that if young male birds are exposed to mercury, if they eat food contaminated with mercury,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: then the songs they produce aren't as complex as those produced by other birds.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says songs from birds exposed to mercury *'aren't as complex'* as other songs — **'aren't as complex'** means **'less complex'**. So the answer is **complex**.

audioscript.text: So quite low-level exposure to mercury is likely to have an impact on male birds in a natural situation, because it can mean that they're less attractive to female birds.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And so it can affect their chances of reproduction.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says less complex songs can *'affect their chances of reproduction'* — the question says this may have a negative effect on birds' something. So the answer is **reproduction**.

audioscript.text: Now, the way she's carrying out this research is worth thinking about.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: She's using a mixture of studies, using birds kept in laboratories, and studies carried out outdoors in the wild.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The lab-based studies have the advantage that you don't get all the variables you would in a natural setting.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So the experimenter has a much higher level of control, and that means they can be more confident about their results in some ways.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says in lab studies the experimenter has a *'much higher level of control'* — the question says lab studies allow more something. So the answer is **control**.

audioscript.text: And of course, they don't have to worry about going out and finding the birds in order to observe them.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So, what are the implications here for humans?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Well, because many birds are migratory, they may be transporting mercury far from contaminated sites, for example.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's been found that ducks who'd been feeding at a contaminated site were later shot by hunters over 1,000 km away.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says *'ducks who'd been feeding at a contaminated site were later shot by hunters'* — the question asks for migrating birds such as something. So the answer is **ducks**.

audioscript.text: And presumably eaten, but these birds likely had mercury levels high enough to warrant concern for human consumption.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In addition, going back to song learning by birds, we saw that this may be affected by mercury contamination.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Well, we also know that in humans, mercury causes developmental delays in the acquisition of language, and in fact this process is very similar in the brain regions it involves.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says mercury causes *'developmental delays in the acquisition of language'* in humans — **'acquisition of language'** means **'learning language'**. The question says mercury causes problems in learning something. So the answer is **language**.

audioscript.text: And even the genes that are involved.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But mercury contamination has other important implications for humans as well.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's now known that an unborn child can be affected if the food eaten by its mother contains high levels of mercury, and these effects can be quite substantial.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says an unborn child can be affected if *'the food eaten by its mother contains high levels of mercury'* — the question says mercury in a mother's body from something may affect the child. So the answer is **food**.

audioscript.text: In the end, it comes down to whether more value is placed on human economic well-being or environmental well-being.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's true, there are new regulations for mercury emissions from power plants.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But these will need billions of dollars to implement and increase costs for everyone.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says new regulations will *'increase costs for everyone'* — the question says new regulations will affect everyone's energy something. So the answer is **costs**.

audioscript.text: Some argue that's too much to pay to protect wildlife.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But as we've seen, the issues go beyond that, and I think it's an issue we need to consider very carefully.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is the end of Section 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

audioscript.text: Uh huh.

audioscript.text: Section 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about noise in cities.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: This lecture will be about the science of acoustics, the study of sound in relation to urban environments such as cities.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As an acoustic engineer myself I think this is an area where we're likely to see great changes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In the past, researching urban soundscapes was simple.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We measured levels of sound in decibels.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So I used to take my sound meter, and I measured the noise somewhere.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And then I might ask a sample of people to say at what level the sound became annoying.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: With data like this, acoustic engineers have been able to build up what we call noise maps, maps of the sound environment, but actually these aren't a lot of use.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: What they do show is that the highest noise levels are generally on roads.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Well, that's not really very surprising.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But there's quite a lot going on that these maps don't show, because they can't capture the complex way that sound varies over time.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So they ignore important issues such as the noise someone might hear from the open windows or gardens of their neighbors, and this sort of noise can be quite significant in summer.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says noise maps ignore sounds from *'open windows or gardens of their neighbors'* — the question asks about noise when *'people's neighbours are in their'* something. The missing word is **'gardens'** — the passage uses the exact same word. So the answer is **gardens**.

audioscript.text: We don't have any databases on this sort of information.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As well as that, these records of sound levels take no account of the fact that people vary in their perceptions of noise.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So someone like me with years of working in acoustics might be very different from you in that regard, but anyway, even though these noise maps are fairly crude, they've been useful in providing information and raising awareness that noise matters.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We need to deal with it, and so it's a political matter.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says *'we need to deal with it, and so it's a political matter'* — **'matter'** means **'issue'**. The question says noise is a **'issue'** that must be dealt with. So the answer is **political**.

audioscript.text: And that's important.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We need rules and regulations, because noise can cause all sorts of problems.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Those of you who are city dwellers know that things go on 24 hours a day, so city dwellers often suffer from interrupted sleep.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's also known that noise can lead to a rise in levels of stress.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Due to physical changes in the body, affecting the composition of the blood.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And there are other problems as well, for instance, if school children don't have a quiet place to study.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says if children don't have a quiet place to study, *'their work will suffer'* — **'work'** here means their school tasks. The question asks about the effect on the **'of schoolchildren'** — the missing word is **'work'**. So the answer is **work**.

audioscript.text: Their work will suffer.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says if children don't have a quiet place to study, *'their work will suffer'* — **'work'** here means their school tasks. The question asks about the effect on the **'of schoolchildren'** — the missing word is **'work'**. So the answer is **work**.

audioscript.text: Now one problem with decibel measurement is that it doesn't differentiate between different types of noise.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Some types of sounds that most people would probably think of as nice and relaxing.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Might well score quite highly in decibel levels.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Think of the sound made by a fountain in a town square, for example.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage gives an example of a pleasant sound: *'the sound made by a fountain in a town square'* — the question asks for the sound of a **'in a town'**. The missing word is **'fountain'** — the passage uses the exact same word. So the answer is **fountain**.

audioscript.text: That's not necessarily something that we'd want to control or reduce.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So maybe researchers should consider these sorts of sounds in urban design.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This is going to be tricky, because just measuring decibel levels isn't going to help us here.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Instead, many researchers are using social science techniques, studying people's emotional response to sound by using questionnaires and so on.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says researchers are using *'social science techniques'* like questionnaires — **'techniques'** means **'methods'**. The question asks about methods from **'sciences'** — the missing word is **'social'**. So the answer is **social**.

audioscript.text: So what exactly do people want to hear in an urban environment?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Some recent interdisciplinary research has come out with results that at first sight seem contradictory.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A city needs to have a sense of activity, so it needs to be lively, with sounds like the clack of high heels on a pavement, or the hiss of a coffee machine.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says a city *'needs to be lively'* with sounds of activity — the question asks for urban environments which are **'but also allow people to relax'**. The missing word is **'lively'** — the passage uses the exact same word. So the answer is **lively**.

audioscript.text: But these mustn't be too intrusive, because at the same time, we need to be able to relax.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One of the major problems in achieving this will be getting architects and town planners to use the research, apart from studying the basics of acoustics.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: These people receive very little training in this area, but in fact, they should be regarding sound as an opportunity to add to the experience of urban living.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says architects and planners *'receive very little training in this area'* — **'very little'** means **'not much'**. The question says they *'do not get much'* in acoustics — the missing word is **'training'**. So the answer is **training**.

audioscript.text: Whereas at present, they tend to see it as something to be avoided or reduced as far as possible, or something that's just a job for engineers, like the street drainage system.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: What's needed is for noise in cities to be regarded as an aesthetic quality, as something that has the qualities of an art form.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: If we acknowledge this, then we urgently need to know what governs it, and how designers can work with it.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We need to develop a complex understanding of many factors.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: What is the relationship between sound and culture?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage asks *'What is the relationship between sound and culture?'* — **'relationship'** means **'relates to'**. The question asks how sound relates to **''** — the missing word is **'culture'**. So the answer is **culture**.

audioscript.text: What can we learn from disciplines such as psychology about the way that sound interacts with human development and social relationships?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And the way that sound affects our thoughts and feelings.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Can we learn anything from physics about the nature of sound itself?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage asks if physics can teach us about *'the nature of sound itself'* — the question asks if physics can help us understand the **'of sound'**. The missing word is **'nature'** — the passage uses the exact same word. So the answer is **nature**.

audioscript.text: Today's powerful technologies can also help us. To show us their ideas, and help us to imagine the effect their buildings will have, architects and town planners already use virtual reality - but these programs are silent.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says virtual reality programs *'are silent'* — **'silent'** means no sound. The question says the current disadvantage is they are **''** — the missing word is **'silent'**. So the answer is **silent**.

audioscript.text: In the future, such programs could use realistic sounds, meaning that soundscapes could be explored before being built.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So hopefully, using the best technology we can lay our hands on, the city of the future will be a pleasure to the ears as well as the eyes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is the end of Section 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
